Canonical priority is not justified merely by inclusion in the Bible; applying ordinary historical criteria leaves virtually all rival gospels historically unreliable, with only some sayings in Thomas possibly tracing to Jesus.
The answer rejects the popular suppression thesis while grounding canonical priority in historical evaluation, thereby defining which traditions merit serious evidentiary weight in the debate.
The claim that numerous rival gospels had claims equal to the canonical texts but were later suppressed for political or theological reasons.

The Gospels preserve some historically credible words and deeds of Jesus, but cannot be read straightforwardly as what happened because they contradict one another, were anonymously written decades later by non-eyewitnesses, and transmit changing oral stories.

This is the principal skeptical case about Gospel reliability, combining a limited concession of recoverable history with the central mechanisms by which memory, transmission, and authorship reduce confidence.

Historians cannot establish miracles such as walking on water because ordinary historical criteria favor explanations involving invented or altered stories over events without recorded precedent, even though the miracle is not declared impossible.

This supplies the methodological basis for withholding historical confidence from resurrection and miracle claims: historical judgment compares explanatory probabilities and cannot establish an unprecedented supernatural event.
